title: Geysers: Nature's Innuendo
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how geysers work: the three components (water supply from percolating rain and snowmelt, a plumbing system of fissures sealed with silica from rhyolite, and a heat source from shallow volcanic or magmatic activity), and how pressure builds, superheats the water, and then flashes to steam to erupt. They contrast geysers with hot springs, describe cone and fountain geysers, and cover Old Faithful's bimodal eruption schedule, famous geysers (Grand Geyser, Steamboat, Strokkur, Geysir in Iceland, Wairakei's Waimangu-area Wairoa/Waimangu geyser), the 1903 Waimangu Valley deaths in New Zealand, and human threats such as geothermal energy production and mineral extraction in Chile. The episode closes with a listener mail about labor unions and the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire, a plug for a Brooklyn city council campaign, and a brief Prince name-change anecdote.

segments.title: Opening banter and geyser misconceptions
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, joke about the sponsor, and say they were wrong about some geyser facts they thought they knew.

segments.title: Deadly Waimangu Valley geyser accident
segments.summary: The hosts recount the 1903 incident in New Zealand's Waimangu Valley where four tourists were killed by a geyser eruption and carried over a mile away.

segments.title: Geyser rarity and the three components
segments.summary: There are roughly a thousand geysers worldwide, in about fifty fields, with Yellowstone holding many. Geysers share a water supply, a plumbing system, and a heat source, along with related features like fumaroles, mud pots, and steam vents.

segments.title: Water supply, heat source, and rhyolite plumbing
segments.summary: Water comes from rain and snowmelt percolating down over thousands of years to near-surface heat from volcanic activity. Fissures in the plumbing are sealed with silica from rhyolite, which keeps the system watertight and allows pressure to build.

segments.title: Pressure, superheating, and eruption
segments.summary: Obstructions and the weight of deep water create pressure that raises the boiling point. Water superheats until it flashes to steam when pressure releases, causing an eruption. The hosts compare this to a pressure cooker and to steaming vegetables. Hot springs differ because they lack an obstruction.

segments.title: Old Faithful eruption schedule and types of geysers
segments.summary: Old Faithful erupts on a bimodal schedule, either long (over four minutes) or short (about two and a half minutes), with roughly an hour or an hour and a half between eruptions. Cone geysers, fountain geysers, and the Grand Geyser are described, with Steamboat and the Waimangu cone geyser mentioned as tall examples.

segments.title: Famous geysers and human threats
segments.summary: Strokkur and Geysir in Iceland are discussed, including Geysir as the oldest known geyser. Earthquakes cut geysers off, geothermal energy production has reduced geyser activity, and mineral extraction in Chile in 2003 killed a geyser field.

segments.title: Naming geysers and Prince anecdote
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh joke about dormant geysers still being called geysers, then shift to a tangent about Prince's name change and contract dispute with Sony.

segments.title: Listener mail on labor unions and Triangle Shirtwaist Fire
segments.summary: A former New York City union organizer praises the labor unions episode and says the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire deserved more coverage. The hosts read a plug for a Brooklyn City Council campaign and invite politicians to send their viewpoints.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with contact information and a sponsor sign-off.
